text_fidelity_a:
MUSE S: The Brain Sensing Headband - Overnight Sleep Tracker & Meditation Headset Device - Multi Sensor Monitor with Responsive Sound Feedback Guidance from Brain Wave, Heart, Body & Breath Activity I have mixed feelings about this Muse S device. First, i know meditation techniques are definitely beneficial in terms of stress, focus, etc. and anything that helps promote it is a good thing. Second, this thing works... plain and simple. It senses what's going on in your head and reacts accordingly - it responds with audible changes in your soundscape, blustery weather sounds when your attention strays, birds chirping when you're properly mindful, etc. Third, it's very comfortable, the head band is soft, adjustable. It sets up without difficulty and finding the right position on my head has never been a problem.

So why the mixed feelings?

To use it, you turn it on, then place it on your head. You hook up some headphones to your phone (either pair them or plug them in), and put them on. Then you open the muse app and pair your headband device. Then you select the program you want to use... there's choices for heart, stress, mind, etc. The differences seem to be in their audio choices and what gets feedback... if its monitoring your heart, for example, it has pounding drums and the feedback encourages lowered heart rates.

This all sounds pretty cool, but after a few tries, it seems like getting set up and settled is just a little more tedious than it needs to be. Perhaps if there were an audio source of some kind built in the band itself, to eliminate a step or two...

Also, if you want to do something other than those specific, functional, non-guided programs, there are some guided meditations available, but those are only available for a monthly or an annual fee. Personally, I'd like to try the guided meditations - it would be nice to at least get a sampling.

Like I said... meditation generally works for me and this product works... the whole idea is pretty cool, but will it get a lot of use? That remains to be seen.
text_fidelity_b: MUSE S: The Brain Sensing Headband - Overnight Sleep Tracker & Meditation Headset Device - Multi Sensor Monitor with Responsive Sound Feedback Guidance from Brain Wave, Heart, Body & Breath Activity

text_fidelity_a:
Precor 9.23 Treadmill with Ground Effects Technology I decided to pick one of these up from a local dealer about two months ago because I hate going to the gym. I reasoned that if I had a treadmill in my apartment, I would have NO more excuses when it came to working out. Luckily, this has paid off for me - I've used the treadmill nearly every day since it was delivered. I really love this treadmill so far.

The Precor was more expensive than similar models, but they seem to have a better reputation when it comes to quality, reliability, customer service, and repairs when things DO go wrong.

When I was testing out treadmills at the store, the Precor definitely did feel more sturdy and well built, even though it's one of their cheaper, Chinese made models. And even though the 9.23 is made in China, I was told that replacement parts are stocked in the US (if that means anything to anyone).

I use my treadmill for walking on an incline only. The manual says that it supports users up to 550 pounds for walking only, and 350 pounds for running (which is much higher than other, cheaper models). I started using the treadmill when I was about 330 pounds, and have never had any major problems with it (I'm down 8 pounds last time I checked). The motor doesn't jerk or hesitate at all, even for someone as heavy as me.

One thing to note regarding the maximum weight: the dealer told me to add 50 pounds to the maximum if you're going to run, so I would have exceeded the 350 pound max if I had done so. This didn't bother me though as I had only planned on walking at an incline anyway.

The only minor issue I've had so far is a slight bit of belt slippage under my right foot. There isn't anything in the manual about this, but after doing some research, I figured out how to tighten the belt a bit so this wouldn't happen. The belt would also go off center as well due to it being too loose. I haven't had a problem since tightening it.

The manual talks about centering the belt using the bolt on the right side of the belt only. To tighten the belt, you just have to do equal clockwise turns on each side of the belt while the treadmill is set to around 3 MPH - maybe a quarter or eighth turn at a time making sure the belt stays centered. I was very conservative about this, testing for slippage after each small turn, and I didn't have to tighten the belt much. This was pretty easy, but Precor will have the local repair people come out if you are at all uncomfortable doing this yourself.

I also called Precor customer service about the belt slippage just to be safe, and I also wanted to see how that whole process would go. When I called, I got connected to someone in the US nearly right away. The customer service agent directed me to the local repair guy, who confirmed what I had found about tightening the belt (he didn't need to come out). The agent seemed rather knowledgable about the product, and cleared up some wrong information I got from the dealer as well. So far, I'm pretty happy with Precor customer service.

The dealer told me I'd need to lubricate the belt, but the manual for the 9.23 says you never need to do this. Customer service confirmed that the 9.23's belt does NOT need to be lubricated.

The sound of the treadmill running and my footsteps are rather loud, but nothing too annoying when you wear headphones and listen to music. If others are in the room, it might be disturbing to them though.

The treadmill has a rather strong odor to it at first that DOES seem to diminish over time. The best way I can describe it is a plastic and/or electronics smell. It's not terrible, but it's not exactly lovely either.

The electronics are ultra basic - just what I wanted. You get a few programs and start, stop, incline and speed controls and that's it. I actually prefer this since I only ever use manual controls anyway, and I have other gadgets I use to do anything fancy.

The 9.23 doesn't have side rails, which is a bit uncomfortable at first, but I've gotten used to it. The next model up has rails and a few other things, but I didn't think it was worth the extra cost even though I really would prefer rails in order to steady myself. This is a minor issue that I've learned to live with.

There is a small ledge under the screen that's perfect for a Kindle or a tablet. I have a [[ASIN:B00HWMPSFQ Samsung Galaxy Tab Pro 10.1 Tablet (Black)]], and it sits securely on the ledge even at 6% incline. I listen to music and use the Kindle app to read, or I listen to Audible audiobooks, and the time flies by. I have little trouble motivating myself to walk in the mornings.

The treadmill has a built-in heart rate monitor when you grip the handles. I have found this to be practically useless though, as the reading jumps up and down way too much, and it takes way too long to get a reading. I wanted to track heart rate, so I bought the Polar H7 heart rate sensor and paired it to my phone, and I use the Polar Beat app to track heart rate, time, and calories burned. So far I'm really loving this system.

The last thing I'll mention has more to do with modern circuit breakers than the treadmill itself. When I first got the treadmill, turning it on would trip adjacent breakers if there was a certain load above maybe around 100 watts on it, like a bathroom light and fan for example. I had never heard of a device tripping a DIFFERENT circuit breaker, but apparently this is very common with treadmills.

Apparently, treadmill motors emit some type of interference that trips newer types of circuit breakers (AFCI). Luckily there is an easy fix for this - all you have to do is plug the treadmill into a [[ASIN:B0000513O4 Tripp Lite ISOBAR4ULTRA Isobar Surge Protector Metal 4 Outlet 6 feet Cord 3330 Joules]] or something similar. I've also tried the [[ASIN:B0000510R4 Tripp Lite ISOBLOK2-0 2-Outlet Isobar Premium Surge Protector 1410 Joules]] but it didn't work. I know other similar surge protectors with EFI/RFI line noise filtering have been reported to work too, but I've only tried the Tripp Lite.

Overall, I'm really glad I spent the extra money on the Precor. It feels sturdy and meets my basic needs, and I have confidence that if I do have a problem, I'll be able to get it taken care of without a ton of hassle.
text_fidelity_b: Precor 9.23 Treadmill with Ground Effects Technology

text_fidelity_a:
SKLZ Reactive Catch Trainer for Improving Hand-Eye Coordination & Speed I assumed this was a bit gimmick and didn't have high hopes. Kiddo is going to be 9 next month and his catch skills are terrible. He and his dad have been working on it, but he is much better at throwing a ball then catching one. He also does well with footwork like in soccer, but man the catching is just sad. I try to help by tossing him small things in the house and usually they just land on the floor and he gives me an irritated "What the heck mom" look. Err, he also has taken several softballs and footballs to the face, when they practice outside, eeek.

So I saw this and figured it couldn't hurt. We played a slow paced soft toss indoor version with the three of us for him to get the hang of it. The tosser would name a color, then give a gentle underhand lob (no spin) and the catcher would have to grab that color. The next day the two of them took it outside for a bit more distance and because I didn't want things getting broken...

Fast-forward a week and I toss a tinfoil ball to him to throw away and he snatches it with one hand (his left no less, he's a righty) like some sorta ninja. Now I'm not saying its not also part luck but there is NO WAY that would have happened a week ago. The look on his face was all smiles instead of the usual glare I get when I toss him stuff and it hits the floor.

This really does help the brain relearn catching to focus on the item to catch rather than the one tossing it. His confidence boost has also been a big help in getting him to want to practice catching in general.

I'm one happy momma and give this a very enthusiastic 5 stars, particularly if you have kiddo in need of some help with catching.
text_fidelity_b: SKLZ Reactive Catch Trainer for Improving Hand-Eye Coordination & Speed

text_fidelity_a:
Arrow Precision Inferno Wildfire Crossbow Package (225-Pounds) I've been hunting with Mathews compound bows for 20 years and reached a point in my age that I wanted to switch to a crossbow. I wanted to find the best bow for the money to start out. I like compounds but I wanted to stay as basic and simple as I could with the crossbow for service and maintaining accuracy so I wanted a recurve.
Long story short the Excaliburs are nice but to rich for my blood so I took a chance on the Wildfire II based on the reviews. I'm glad that I did.
Pros:
Excellent fit and finsh work on the entire bow. Definitely quality construction on par with any of the big name crossbow makers.
It seems as fast and they say it is. Once sighted in it is consistently accurate. I think this bow is on par with the Excalibur baseline bows Like the Axiom or Ibex if not better as this bow has a one peice Aluminum rail versus a plastic rail. Weight is not bad at all and it feels well balanced for free hand shooting. Soft touch Camo is awesome and a nice balance of pattern and color.
Thumb Safety just like a rifle. Not up on the side of the string latch like a lot of other crossbows and quiet as a mouse. Not a loud CLICK! when you take the safety off. The trigger does have some creep but is pretty smooth overall. The more I shoot the better it gets.
Shot noise is average and less than a pellet gun for comparison. It comes with factory installed limb dampeners that attach to the riser/limb. I also installed the SIMS LIMBSAVER kit and it definitely helped reduce the sound when fired.
Scope is actually very good quality and clarity. Super clean reticle and the adjustable illumination is great for early morning/late evening shots! I was thinking to buy a Nikon but this scope is really nice so I will keep using it.
Rope cocker, Arrows, quiver, and sling are very nice quality as well. Super sling swivels too!
Must haves:
Plano Soft bow case. Best priced case that actually fits the bow another really good option is the OMP Crossbow soft case. A little more in cost but has additional pockets for arrows etc.
Tenpoint ACUrope cocker (BEST). Compact and retractable. Works like a dream and has a belt pouch.
Carbon Express Bolts. Either the Piledrivers or if you want the best get the Maxima Hunters. Buy their lighted nocks for your hunting arrows.
Go ahead and buy the MTM bolt case for your extra bolts.
Scorpion Venom string wax. The bow comes with string wax but I feel the Scorpion is easier to use and stays super slick in all weather.
Rail lube. DO NOT USE STRING WAX! I did and it slowed down the bow and killed my accuracy. I had to clean the rail with rubbing alcohol and start over. Buy Excalibur rail lube and/or do some research on the bow forums on what the veteran shooters are using. Some recommend silicone spray and other types of lube. If you're going to hunt use something that doesn't have any odor. I ended up using Ultralube 4x. It's all natural and no odor.
NAP 100 grain Sptifire Edge mechanical broadheads. These are my personal favorite and for overall accuracy I prefer mechanicals over fixed blades for better flight at high speeds.
Target for field point is the Hurricane H25 hands down best practice target for the money. It stops the bolts no matter what and is heavy and stable. You don't need a stand for it.
Target for broadheads I recommend the Blobtarget or American white tale HybriMAT AP . They are both pricey (BT 18"x18"x10" $90 shppied) (HybriMAT AP 18"x18"x12" $129.95 shipped) but they will last you for years and years vs the cheaper ones that last a year and are still very expensive!
Update:
Bought a Prochrono on Amazon to check the speed of the bow and right now it is 315fps with the stock arrows and with the Maxima Hunters. Dyna Flight string should bring it up to as much as 330fps.
I ended up removing the limbsavers since they slowed it down (10fps!) and actually created vibration in the bow after the shot. To be honest the noise level is not much different without them.
Another update. Bow is shooting 330fps using Carbon Express 20" hunter maximas and 100gr tips. I switched to Black Eagle Spynal Tapp arrows and the speed is still on.
Final deer season tally is 3 does and i buck
text_fidelity_b: Arrow Precision Inferno Wildfire Crossbow Package (225-Pounds)

text_fidelity_a:
TechKen Solar Bulbs Lights Outdoor 2 Sets Soft White Non-Dimmable No Need Energy for Outdoor Securtiy Camping Light We have occasional power failures and sometimes candles and lamps are not enough to do some tasks, especially when the task at hand needs a bit bright light. Let's see how these work.

WHAT ARE THESE LIKE?
This comes in a set of two bulbs that have a hook on top. There are two panels for solar charging that come with the bulbs. I hang them in the window to charge, and then when it is time to use them, they push into the bulb and you have light.

HOW DO THESE PERFORM?
These lights are great for a couple hours of light. They give light about like a 40 watt bulb or so. It is pretty white light too so it does enable me to see in the dark.

WHERE DO I USE THESE?
POWER OUTAGE
There are a few uses for these. First I keep them charged in the window so that if we have a power outage, especially if it lasts a while, we are ready to have some light if needed.

OUTDOOR SHED
I also use these in my shed. I have a shed with no electricity. There are two windows, so I can also use these to have light with the panels in the window during the day, or at night to get some light for a couple of hours.

CAMPING
If you are camping these are also very helpful. You just have to be careful that they don't get soaking wet when recharging just to be sure.

THE BOTTOM LINE
For a great way to have some light that resembles electric light during power outages, I am glad to have these handy. They seem to hold a charge nicely and light up well. I have not had to DEPEND on them for extended time, but they are great to fill in with important light needs during a power outage or in a location where there is no electricity.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS. I love having these around and would buy them again if needed.

WildHorn Outfitters Quick-Up Cabana Style XL Beach Tent– 2 in 1 Sun Canopy and Summer Shelter– Perfect for Family Outings, Camping Trips, Or Lakeside Activities I've used several other sun shades at the beach and at soccer games. This is in a category all of its own. This is an easy-setup tent that opens entirely or closes for privacy and camping. The door turns into a massive sun shade that can be adjusted in height. Attachable mesh panels offer shade from the side while maintaining visibility.

Pros:
Size - Larger than the Litespeed Quick Shelter. Much more shade. The Litespeed needs to be oriented in the correct direction for it to provide shade. Also, packs down into a good size for a large tent. You can actually fit the tent back into the bag it comes in.
Setup - Wildhorn includes good video explanations for setup and takedown but it was hardly needed. Setup was a breeze and there were no bow-and-arrow style pull cords.
Shade - The amount of shade this provides is far superior to other canopies like the Litespeed Quick Shelter. The Quick Shelter includes a large tarp to sit on but it isn't covered by the shelter. this provides more shade but only has a floor inside the tent.
Multipurpose - Can be used as a standalone tent. I couldn't get my kids out of it. They wanted to camp in it as soon as I set it up.
Privacy - This closes up entirely when you want it closed. You can put a napping child in the tent and close the door while playing at the beach. You can close it up and change clothes. You can close it up and keep valuables inside where prying eyes can see them. You can also open the giant door and windows to keep cool in the shade.
Adjustable Shade - Unlike other shelters you can adjust how high/low the sunshade rests. The poles are adjustable and you can simply roll up the door if you don't want to bother with poles.

Cons:
Great in sand but need more equipment for the backyard- If you plan on using this on solid ground you are going to want better stakes (the stakes aren't necessary unless it's windy). Also, If you want to use the poles to extend the sun shade you need to do it in the sand with the included pole holders (if you use a little rope and a stake you could do this on the ground but rope isn't included).
Take-down - There is a small trick to packing up the tent. Not difficult, but I recommend watching the video to avoid frustration.

Overall, a great shelter. Excited to take it to the beach in the summer.
text_fidelity_b: WildHorn Outfitters Quick-Up Cabana Style XL Beach Tent– 2 in 1 Sun Canopy and Summer Shelter– Perfect for Family Outings, Camping Trips, Or Lakeside Activities

text_fidelity_a:
Gaiam Sol Sticky-Grip Yoga Mat (5mm) I admit, I have a bit of a "thing" with trying new yoga mats. I have a mat that I love and that I use for most purposes, including practicing both at home and in class, which is my [[ASIN:B00AB3LLVS Manduka eKo Lite Yoga Mat]]. However, I also own other mats I use for other purposes, such as keeping one at work, one for Pilates, etc.

I was interested in this Gaiam mat because it is thicker than my eKo Lite, 5mm as compared to 3mm. Although I like my think Manduka, I thought than the thicker Gaiam mat might be good for occasions when I have to practice on particularly hard flooring. Upon unrolling the mat, I did like that it was thick but FIRM--i.e., it was not squishy. This mat is designed to be two-sided. The first side, which has a texture, is described as the more "traditional" side. At first, I thought that this side would provide more stability, but as soon as I stepped on it, I found that my feet were sliding around.

Given this, I decided to try the mat on the smooth side, which is the design side. This side definitely had more of a "sticky" feel. Upon first use, my feet felt secure upon the mat: the mat did feel like a "sticky mat," and my standing poses felt good. Therefore, I decided to take the mat with me to yoga class the next day, which was a free class held in a room with concrete floors. Just getting the mat there was a bit of a feat, as 1) the mat was a VERY tight fit in my [[ASIN:B000VW4VWA Manduka MatSak Yoga Bag]] (designed for full-size Manduka mats), and 2) the mat is much heavier than my eKo light. But worse, taking the mat to class was a mistake. Initially, standing poses were okay, but my hands continually slid on the mat in down dog. Furthermore, as the mat got a bit sweaty, it just got more slippery and felt quite unsafe.

This is a pretty mat and feels to be very high quality. I may continue to use it at home for Pilates and abs work, but due to stability problems, I cannot recommend it for yoga.
text_fidelity_b: Gaiam Sol Sticky-Grip Yoga Mat (5mm)

text_fidelity_a:
Extremus Rendu Soft Cooler, 12/20/30 Can Updated Insulated Cooler Bag, Portable and Waterproof Beach Cooler with 100% Leakproof Zipper, Large Capacity for Fishing, Kayaking, Camping, Beaches & Trips We buy our milk from a special farmer that only does grass fed milk. It is not too bad usually, except in the summer, it is tough to keep the milk cold as we go to and from the farm as it is not near our home. This cooler answers that problem.

HOW TO OPEN
This comes with a zipper and an extra pull included. I can see why. This zipper is quite difficult to use. The pack includes a lubrication tube and tells you how to keep the zipper working. Well, I did it several times and it still is not easy to slide the zipper.

INSIDE
The inside is quite a bit smaller than the outside due to the insulation. Our milk bottles will only fit long ways instead of sideways as I thought they would.

DOES IT KEEP THINGS COLD?
I have to say that I got some yogurt the other day and did not have ice to put in the cooler. I put in 3 containers of yogurt which were quart sized. I had them in there for about 5 hours. When I got home, the yogurt was still pretty cold. I am impressed.

STRAPS/HANDLE
The straps and handle on this cooler are really great. The shoulder strap makes it easy for me to carry this along with the other things I have to carry in the house It is comfortable and works out well.

LEAKS?
This did not leak so far when ice melts.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This is the perfect cooler for getting our milk this summer. It will allow me to make the trip and not be so concerned about keeping the milk cold in our other coolers because this one with some ice included will work perfectly.

MY RATING
FIVE STARS although the zipper on this is very frustrating and I would like to take off a star, but I don't think it is that bad at this point. I will update of anything changes.
text_fidelity_b: Extremus Rendu Soft Cooler, 12/20/30 Can Updated Insulated Cooler Bag, Portable and Waterproof Beach Cooler with 100% Leakproof Zipper, Large Capacity for Fishing, Kayaking, Camping, Beaches & Trips

text_fidelity_a:
Fox Outdoor Products Mission Ready Drop Leg Holster I wanted to try a drop leg holster for some time and came across this model in desert camo through another vendor. For the price, and because I had heard good things about Fox, I decided to take advantage of the reduced price and see how good (or bad) this holster really is.

The first day, after strapping it on and making all the adjustments I could, I carried around a mini ball peen hammer just to try to get used to it. Why did I choose a hammer? While I am CCW licensed, Florida does not currently allow "open carry". So I had to put something of measurable weight in the holster without alarming the neighbors or anyone driving by on our street. I could imagine someone seeing me with a drop leg holster and calling our local law enforcement, not knowing that their was no gun in the holster -- but assuming there was.Yes, the weight of the hammer head made the holster cant backwards, so I switched to a rubber mallet. This provided a much better balance.

Then I switched to a Glock 23 and a Springfield XD-45 MOD 2 and alternately carried both around inside our home, After trying my darndest to get it to fit properly, I came to the following conclusions:

1. This is a cool looking and well constructed rig. The desert camo design is well done, the material is light and flexible, and the various
clips, belts and fasteners work like they should.
2 The holster accommodated both the Springfield and Glock perfectly and the strap easily fastened over the gun butt.
3. It is very light and designed to fit comfortably against your thigh.
4. And of course it easily carries a lighter weight weapon like a Kahr PM9 and a Glock 42. In fact the smaller and lighter pistols eliminate
the bounding around explained below. But who wants to carry a "pocket pistol" in a drop leg holster?

But, and this is a "big but" for me, the single strap that fastens the holster around your thigh just couldn't keep the holster secure and steady. It bounced while walking and really moved around when running (even at my slow pace). I tightened the thigh strap so that over 14" of strap was outside the buckle, but it just never felt secure. No one wants that feeling -- you want your gun to be right where it's supposed to be -- all of the time.

This holster really needs two improvements: 1. It needs a second strap to go around the thigh, one high and one low. 2. It also needs more vertical adjustment so that it can be carried a bit higher on your belt. Both of these changes would result in a better fit and should eliminate excess movement.
text_fidelity_b: Fox Outdoor Products Mission Ready Drop Leg Holster

There is a wire inside each of these that connects to the battery box.)

I felt just the faintest bit of warmth from one sock and nothing from the other. I put them on and honestly could not tell a difference between the non-working side and the one that was faintly warm. I thought perhaps they needed more time to warm up, so I continued wearing them hoping that would happen. I was busy working and after a couple of hours realized that they had never warmed up. So I decided to check the batteries, 'just in case,' they weren't fully charged. When I checked them on my battery tester, all four were completely dead even though I had gotten them from my fresh supply. I wondered if they could possibly have been bad to begin with, though that seemed highly unlikely. Then I wondered if the box had somehow drained the batteries.

Still holding out a tiny bit of hope the socks would warm, I got out more batteries. This time I checked them with my battery tester first, to make sure they were fully charged. They were. Again I felt the tiniest bit of warmth and thought, "Great! I guess the last batch of batteries were no good."

Put them on and again, could not feel the warmth. I later checked the fully charged batteries and .. you guessed it, they were drained. So not only did the stupid socks not work, they somehow drained EIGHT AA batteries!! What a waste of time and money. Needless to say, I want to send these back.

It's really a shame because a lot of people would love to have socks like this if they would actually work. I hope the manufacturer figures out a way to make them work AND do so without having to go through dozens of batteries each week.
text_fidelity_b: Electric Battery Operated Heated Socks Men Women Rechargeable Washable for Hunting Winter Skiing Mobile Warming Powered Battery Heated Socks…

text_fidelity_a: KME Precision Knife Sharpening System The main reason I bought this sharpening system over edge pro, wicked edge or tsprof was the fact that it has a handle and I can use it while sitting in my chair watching TV. I know myself and I am waaay more likely to use something like this more often if I can use it while sitting in my chair so this review is based on using it that way. It came with a letter from the company providing ways to contact them directly if there is any issue which is awesome, and the instruction manual was very clear and easy to understand with good pictures. I've always been scared to ruin my factory edges since I have never been able to get them as sharp again so I have been only stropping which works great until you get real damage which I did a few weeks ago when I dropped my ferrum forge gent on the concrete floor at work and chipped the edge. Given it was my first time using this sharpener I'd say it took about 30 minutes to get setup and work the chips out of the edge and go up to 1500 grit. It was a great edge at that point, but you should definitely get the strop that fits in there. It is very sharp at 1500, but the edge isn't really polished at that point. After using the strop that fits in there it not only looks great, but it is an edge that I have never seen from any of my knives before. It is truly scary sharp. Like not popping hair sharp, but no pressure at all and the hairs just go away without even noticing that it happened sharp. I will be redoing the factory edge on all my knives over the next few weeks. The only con I noticed is that it is a bit awkward when changing between stones. You have to be very careful of the knife edge while putting force on the knob that holds the stones in. Speaking of which, you have to get the knob on the stones quite tight for it to stay in place well. Other than those 2 things, which are quite minor (and the first one is almost certainly only due to me doing this in my recliner haha) this thing is freakin amazing. Highly recommended!
text_fidelity_b: KME Precision Knife Sharpening System

HOMGIM Exercise Bike [[VIDEOID:bf4a381ea2346e023f15723581aa57ec]] This bike is easy to set up and adjust, and it has lots of features that make it a useful addition to my fitness program. I've uploaded a short video showing the adjustments and features, but I'll run thru them quickly here, too. Let me know if you find anything here useful.

You'll want to set the seat height so that your thigh) (hip to knee) is parallel to the ground at the top of the rotation. Then slide the seat back to where it's an easy reach forward to the handlebars without holding a lot of your weight there.

The tension on the pedals is adjusted by a big black knob just below the handlebars. There are also separate tensioned handles that you can pull to get an upper body (arms, shoulders, back, and abs) workout as you ride.

You can scroll through various screens on the electronic display. The best of these, in my opinion, is a heart rate monitor that reads your pulse while your hands are on the handlebar sensors. You can also get distance, time, and speed traveled. Its really a pretty capable machine, considering the low price.

This little bike folds up when not in use, so you can store it in a closet, lay it on the floor along a wall, or lean it in a corner. It isn't as beefy (or likely as durable) as one of the fancy spinning bikes at the gym, but this one is a lot more affordable, and meets my needs at home just fine. Check out the video, and let me know this was helpful.

text_fidelity_a:
Gaiam Sol Sticky-Grip Yoga Mat (5mm) This yoga mat has a lovely color and attractive patterns embossed in its textured surface. It is well made of high-quality, sustainable, latex-free rubber, and the ribbed bottom works well for preventing slippage on a smooth surface.

This mat out-gassed a slight chemical smell for a few days but it did eventually wear off.

The manufacturer claims this mat is "thick." It seems to me to be about the same thickness, or at best a tiny bit thicker, than the standard rubber mats provided at my gym. For what it is worth, I have this to say about all such mats: If your body doesn't come with it's own built-in "padding," it is a bruising experience to do yoga or calisthenic exercises on a hard floor while sitting or lying on this or any other thin, rubber mat. For that reason, there aren't any yoga mats of this type on the market, including this one, that seem "thick" to me personally. However, since that is a typical design feature among all rubber yoga mats, I am not grading down this mat for not being what I truly consider thick--a depth of three inches. That is the thickness of a different type of yoga mat, a [[ASIN:B003VQNM2I futon mat]], which I also own. The advantage of this mat over a futon mat is that it weighs 5 pounds vs 19 pounds for the futon mat, making it much more portable. It is also substantially easier to keep clean.

Speaking of cleaning this mat, it is not necessary to pay a lot of money for special yoga-mat cleaning solutions when a mat is made of rubber, as this one is. You can make your own quite inexpensively. Here are some examples:

1. Dilute white vinegar in a ratio of 1:16 (1 tablespoon per cup). Vinegar is a natural disinfectant. To increase disinfectant properties, you can add a tablespoon of fresh lemon juice or a few drops of any of the following essential oils which each have disinfectant properties: tea tree, eucalyptus, peppermint, lavender, oregano, lemon, and clove.

2. Dilute a biodegradeable liquid soap, such as [[ASIN:B00016QTYO Sal Suds]], in the same proportion as the white vinegar, 1:16.

3. You can add 1 tablespoon liquid soap to each cup of white-vinegar mixture to maximize cleaning effectiveness.

Instructions for use of cleaning solutions:

1. Put the cleaning solution of your choice in a spray bottle and shake well.

2. Spray the mat and use a clean rag or paper towel to scrub the mat.

3. If you use a soap mixture, you may want to go back over the mat with a clean, damp rag or damp paper towel in order to remove the soap residue. This is not necessary when you use a vinegar mixture.

Note that rubber is not harmed by water. This means that, if you wanted to, you could hose it off on your patio during warm-weather seasons and drape it over a patio chair or the rail of a deck or porch to dry.
text_fidelity_b: Gaiam Sol Sticky-Grip Yoga Mat (5mm)

text_fidelity_a: Fitness by Cathe' Adjustable Max Vest Here goes.. I speed walk almost every day for at 3 sometimes 5 miles. But, that's all that seemed to be a plus for me. On the downside, the vest comes with only one strap which is over my chest area (definitely could have used a bottom strap). I found it extremely uncomfortable while walking, with the vest shifting all around while I walked from foot to foot (and the faster I walked, the worse it got). I was wearing this under my t-shirt with just a sports bra and found it scratchy and irritating and when I sweat, it became extremely uncomfortable. I ended up wearing it over my t-shirt which, although it resolved the scratchy feel to my bare skin and some of the shifting problem, but it made me look dopey as I was walking. In fairness, I rated this a three star. I figure if you are using for mat work (pilates or weights) it would probably do the trick for extra resistance. And, as I mentioned earlier, I realy did like the ability to add and subtract weights to tailor a workout. Would definitely not recommend for walking or running.

Lifestyle by Focus Electric Travel Cooler/Warmer Portable Camping Cooler Hard Cooler Ice Chest Roller Wheeled Cooler for Car, Home, Beach, Fishing, Camping, Party (Blue) Large 48 Quart, Holds 60 cans So far, I am underwhelmed. I purchased this in advance of a cross-country trip and an extended stay in a budget hotel that doesn't have a room fridge - hence the choice of dual power source. Being the prudent sort, I plugged it in at home to see whether it really would cool down to 40 degrees. House was 75 degrees, cooler after running all night was 55 degrees, at best. I'll probably keep it, and maybe as a beer or cola cooler it's fine, but as for being able to keep perishables such as eggs, milk, lunch meat and cheese in the hotel, or in transit for 1000 miles, for that matter, I'm not sure it's worth the risk of food poisoning to rely on its cooling capability. It's also smaller inside than I was expecting.

Update: On a second, and much longer, trip, I took this along, mostly for refrigeration in transit, but then when I reached my destination, I found that the full-size fridge was on the blink, so I plugged this in and it kept stuff reasonably cold, including the return trip, although still not much lower than 40-degrees. All told, some of the stuff I carried with me was still good when I got back home eleven days later, and maybe some of that was due to having also packed big bottles of frozen drinking water (ice) and starting out with other frozen foods; maybe some of it was due to my travel being in weather that was at freezing or below and the cooler rode for part of the trip in an unheated truck boot. All that being said, I still wouldn't be totally reliant on it in the summer, and would still pack the bottled ice - which is also a good way to gauge just how well the cooler is doing its job.

text_fidelity_a:
Nordic Walking Poles for Individuals 6’ 2” – 6’ 3” = 132.5cm SWIX of Norway. All 32 Lengths Coming Soon 1-Piece Non-Collapsible. #1 for Hiking, Trekking, Physical Therapy. My review is primarily geared towards people who are interested in learning the Nordic walking techniques and are looking for inexpensive, appropriate walking sticks. It is also a comparison of the sticks offered here and the so-called “crappy Chinese” anti-shock, telescoping sticks. I have purchased both and am including photos below.

I started Nordic walking about 3 or 4 years ago. At the time, I wasn’t sure that this was something I would continue to do and did not want to spend a small fortune on equipment that would, once again, end up unused in a closet. But I was having trouble walking even a short distance (100 ft. or so) without excruciating burning in my legs and back, so thought I needed to give this a shot. I sprang for the cheap sticks and boy, am I glad I did! Within a few weeks, I was walking a mile with very little discomfort. That distance might be laughable to some, but to me, it was a miracle!

But honestly, it had less to do with the type of sticks than it did with learning the proper technique. There are many videos available that demonstrate the technique and anyone interested should spend some time watching them. It is not difficult to learn. In fact once you get the rhythm it’s like riding a bike…you don’t forget how to do it.

As far as the poles go, I see little difference in them. Perhaps at a higher price difference there is, but it’s still more about learning the skills.

Cheap Chinese poles (the black ones in the photos): When I bought mine I made some modifications. The rubber tips that were included wore out quickly. I replaced those with the boot type of tip which has lasted all these years and many miles. The tips are deeply grooved like snow tires and they do pick up small pieces of sand. This will make them slip some on asphalt, but it’s fairly easy to flick a grain of sand out and continue your walk. I also replaced the sponge rubber grip just below the handle (because it tore easily) with some closed cell tubing that I found online. That wasn’t entirely necessary because you never or rarely grab the poles in that area. I should have just eliminated it altogether.

These poles are the twist lock telescoping type (not the clamp type), which is handy when you don’t know what length pole you need in the beginning. But once adjusted, it is a PITA to collapse or readjust them. They do have a scale on them that shows the length you’ve set them to, so if you get these, make a note or find some way of marking the length. I never collapse mine anymore, because I want to start walking immediately, not fiddle with adjustments. However, if you need to pack your walking sticks, and don’t mind messing with the twist locks, this is certainly a consideration when you buy. I have never had the twist locks fail or accidently collapse once snuggly hand tightened.

These poles also have the anti-shock springs. It makes them heavier and, yes, they make a rattling noise every time the pole hits the pavement. Their extra weight does makes their footfall more forceful. I see no advantage to the springs at this point, but I’ve heard that they are helpful when going down steep terrain. Can’t say, because most of my walking is on fairly level pavement. BUT, DO NOT let the noise stop you from buying if you don’t want to spend a lot of money in the beginning. Getting you walking again is far more important than any minor rattles.

The handle grips are very comfortable and include a strap for your hands to go up through. I found these straps were much more comfortable for me and more convenient to use. Just remember to insert your hand up from the bottom of the strap.

Overall, these poles have a bigger diameter than the “real” ones and are slightly heavier. However, I think the few added ounces actually give you a better upper body and arm workout than the lighter poles. So, to me, the extra weight could be advantageous. Cost for these poles was 14.95 for each pole (@29.90). The Leki replacement tips cost $17.31 with tax, and I highly recommend them. I’m not including the rubber grip which is not necessary, so my actual cost was $47.21 with tax.

Real Nordic walking sticks (blue in the photos): As noted above, these are somewhat lighter, thinner, nonadjustable, non-spring-loaded poles. It is important that you order the right length. They adjustable have glove like straps attached to the handle.

Personally, I’m not entirely pleased with these particular straps. As you will see in the photos, their design leaves something to be desired. I have circled the points where they irritate my hands. And here, I will have to make some kind of modification if I want to use these poles for an extended time. The gloves interfere with wearing my fitness watch and the binding on some corners should be more rounded instead of squared off. Strapping your hand in or out, by means of Velcro strips, is awkward; and should you need to let go of your poles if you fall, you’re out of luck. There is a means of length adjustment (by pulling upward on the handle top) which is lacking in the Chinese poles, but it doesn’t solve the rubbing issues, since the part which cradles your hand doesn’t change position. After I have used these poles more, I may try to fashion a strap comparable to the ones on the Chinese poles.

The handles themselves are thinner and (though you shouldn’t be clasping them tightly) may be more suited to smaller hands. I can’t say for sure, but they are still comfortable.

I have a gut feeling that the boot tips on these sticks will wear quickly, needing to be replaced often. However, they do not have the deep tread of the Leki replacement tips and do not pick up grains of rock or sand, so that is an advantage as far as sliding on pavement goes. I will most likely replace these stock tips with the Leki ones and just deal with the rocks.

The cost for these poles (before any changes I may make) is, at this writing, $77.45 including tax and/or shipping. I am, otherwise, perfectly satisfied with these “real” Nordic walking sticks. They are light, not noisy and do what they’re supposed to do.

Both poles need some slight modification, but their functions are identical. Once again, it’s about technique, not one type of pole compared to another. Please do not let any hype make your decision. It’s far more important that you get out there and start walking.
I'm awarding 5 stars to either kind of pole. Both work pretty much equally.

text_fidelity_a:
Compact Camp Stool Folding Ultralight Portable Mini Chair for Camping Fishing Hiking Gardening Beach Outdoor Chair for Kid Alduts I received this portable camping chair from the manufacturer at no cost for evaluation, and here are my thoughts.

This portable chair is great for camping, backpacking, and attending outdoor events. Weighing les than 2 pounds, it comes in a sturdy storage back with a handle and loops so it can be carried by hand, tucked away with gear, or lashed to a pack without taking much space or adding much weight, and it's so easy to set up my ten year old can do it in about 2 minutes.

The support frame is made of lightweight aircraft aluminum sections attached to each other by shock cord, so you just slip the sections together, secure the ends into the plastic housing, and then attach the ends to the slots in the chair. It's easier if you attach the bottom before the back. When assembled the bottom of the seat is approximately 14" from the ground, the seat is about 21" across, and the back is about 26" high.

I found that the chair sits well on the ground and it feels very stable. The material conforms to the shape of the body so it provides good support, but it does sit very low to the ground so people with arthritis, sciatica, hip problems, or mobility issues might find it difficult to get into or out of without assistance. The chair will support an adult weighting up to 260 pounds, but my 10 year old already decided that it's perfect for her so it's now going to be her chair.

The chair is easy to dissemble and put back in the carry bag, when you're finished using it, and it hardly takes any space at all to store. We really like this chair and think it's perfect for camping, fishing, outdoor concerts or any other outdoor event.
text_fidelity_b: Compact Camp Stool Folding Ultralight Portable Mini Chair for Camping Fishing Hiking Gardening Beach Outdoor Chair for Kid Alduts

text_fidelity_a: Stanley Adventure Stainless Fry Pan Camp Cook Set, 9 Piece Camping Cookware Mess Kit with Stainless Pan, Cooking Utensils, and Dishes So many ways to consider camp cook gear.  This is a  Classic for a reason.  When I was young and fit and backpacked most weekends in the summer and autumn, the difference between stainless steel and titanium was that one metal warped more than the other and one weighed a bit less...but not enough to matter.  Both metals were uneven in the transfer of heat; foods stuck.  We 'loved' our stainless Sierrra Cups...but they were too hot on the lips...and cooled the contents too fast.  This Stanley product with its expanded poly cups provides extended warmth to beverages, soups or stews.  The metal pot has clearly visible volumetric markings.  The cup sits very well on folding alchohol or small wood burning stoves like the Firebox.  'Bug Out Kits' benefit from this setup:  we cannot rely on available wood but we need a pot to boil water and something to eat a small meal in...for two.

text_fidelity_a:
Prevention Easy Healing Stretches: Follow-Along Routines - Guided Stretching routines to Alleviate Pain, Boost Energy, and Feel Amazing Kathi Ross-Nash is a wise, beautiful and elegant instructor who obviously has a lot of experience with Pilates and yoga. She has a slim, toned and strong body and can do exercises with advanced precision. It is a joy to watch her body move through all the poses and stretches and I especially loved how her makeup was done. Her voice and chatty style lulled me into a relaxed state almost like hypnosis. I found her instructions calming and soothing.

Some of the exercises are done in a chair like the face and neck exercises. You will do shoulder shrugs and stretch the neck side to side. Then you will do eye exercises and facial exercises that help relax your jaw. You may find these exercises and stretches especially healing if you work on a computer all day or if you tend to clench your jaw from stress.

Other exercises are done on the floor with a yoga mat. The hip exercises and stretches have some easy and advanced poses that are inspired by Pilates. The leg stretches can be modified with yoga blocks and include active stretching that test endurance and strength. You will move quickly from one pose to another.

For the Feet and Calves you will need a chair and two yoga blocks. If you've never exercised your feet before like this you may want to take the rest of the day off or try the chest openers next.

The Chest stretching was actually one of my favorite parts of this DVD. You will feel your core being strengthened too. You will need a strap - a yoga one works great.

To do some of these stretches you will need to be able to get down onto the floor and back up again. Not so easy for me now that I'm over 50 but I pushed through and did it anyways. So I would say this DVD also tests your resilience and endurance not to mention patience and flexibility. I could have easily done all these exercises with no problem in my 20s, 30s and 40s! So if you do a lot of yoga and Pilates you may find these exercises very relaxing and invigorating.

There is a bar on the left side of the screen to clue you in to how long you still have until completion of each section. It is not distracting once you get used to it and seems helpful.

Some of the props you will need include 2 yoga blocks, a strap, a clean dry washcloth, a rubber band and a small ball for the foot exercises. I managed without the small ball but definitely used the strap and found a rubber band in my drawer that worked. The washcloth is used for the jaw stretches but nowhere else.

Some of my other favorite DVDs for Stretching and Strengthening include:

Simply Stretch by Jessica Smith
Yoga for Inflexible People
Pilates on the Go by Maria Leone
Face Aerobics
Karen Voight Full Body Stretch
Stretch and Strength by Anne Pringle Burnell (Especially geared for those over 50!)

I think it is a worthy goal to collect as many of these excellent DVDs as you can because stretching DVDs are what you need to feel good and flexible as you age. This Easy Healing Stretches DVD has five sections that you can do over a period of days to increase your whole body's strength and tone. Enjoy!

~The Rebecca Review
text_fidelity_b: Prevention Easy Healing Stretches: Follow-Along Routines - Guided Stretching routines to Alleviate Pain, Boost Energy, and Feel Amazing

Fitarc Pull Up Assist Bands,Pull Up Resistance Bands for Chin Up,Adjustable Pullup Bands I remember as a young man I used to be able to do 10 pull ups. 30+ years later, I tried to do a pull-up and couldn't even do one - not even half of one, actually. It's been 6 months, and I am still working on 2. Someone told me that this is because I'm not going through the whole pull-up motion often enough to build the muscles and that I should go to a gym and use a machine that gives you an assist so you can go through repetitions of the whole motion - over time, the assist is then reduced without reducing the number of repetitions. Well, I live too far from a gym - so I got these assist bands. And the first time I tried them after installation, I did 5 pull-ups - and could have done more! Starting tomorrow I will do 10 pull-ups and then reduce the number of straps over time.

The only downside to this solution is that if you don't have your pull-up bars installed high enough, you have to fiddle around with the strap length or put your knees in the stirrup instead of the feet. But that's not the bands' fault.

text_fidelity_a:
AURORAE Classic/Printed Extra Thick and Long Yoga Mat. Slip Free Rosin Included As a yoga beginner, I have few comparisons for this mat, except for the two classes I took before I owned the mat, in which I used mats provided by each respective yoga studio. The studio mats were of "normal" thickness, and although they were sticky enough, they were too thin. The Aurorae mat offered a significant improvement in thickness, although for some poses I still have to use additional padding, such as a blanket (but then everyone in the class is doing that, regardless of the mats they're using).

As the instructions advised, I did thoroughly wash and dry the mat before using it. I washed it with a large sponge in a bathtub filled with very warm water and a few generous squirts of dishwashing detergent. The first time I used the mat after washing it, I noticed my hands slipping a bit during downward dog, so when I got it home, I washed the mat again, and for the second washing I scrubbed the mat's surface with a soft body brush.

That seemed to help, although I suspect if you're sweaty, you'll get some slippage even when the mat's clean. I think it's important to remember to wash your hands (and feet?) before yoga practice, if you want to minimize slippage on the mat.

Overall I'm happy with the product, and I'd buy one again if I needed another mat.
text_fidelity_b: AURORAE Classic/Printed Extra Thick and Long Yoga Mat. Slip Free Rosin Included

text_fidelity_a:
Ultimate Body Press Wall Mounted Doorway Pull Up Bar Wow, what a monster! This ULTIMATE BODY PRESS WALL-MOUNTED DOORWAY PULL UP BAR is a serious piece of exercise equipment--the bar measures 4 inches around. This allows a solid, comfortable, non-tiring grip for large hands. A heavy duty pull up bar like this one is an excellent choice if you have limited space for exercise equipment--you can use it for resistance band exercises as well as for pull ups.

But the bar does require a fair amount of space (an over door space about 38 inches wide). You mount the bar on the solid "king studs" located about 3 inches on each side of most interior doorways. Thus you will need a doorway that allows you to reach those studs. Some of my condo's doorways are set flush against an interior wall on one side, and are totally unsuitable for mounting this bar.

Also, you need ceilings that are high enough to allow you some headroom for pull ups. My condo has 8 foot ceilings, and most of the doorways leave 15 inches above the opening. This is enough room, but just barely. If you use the bar for resistance band training, you need adequate space to move around in front of the doorway, too.

The installation hardware (lag bolts and washers) is included. It is kind of overkill, making these out of titanium when a good chromoly steel of the same weight would be nearly as good. I'm sure a company could make quality steel stakes (albeit a little thinner) that would be just as strong, but I'm digressing, when you go premium, go big, go really big! And these are that.

Unfortunately the listing is kind of messed up and ambiguous. When I received them, as I hoped these are the stakes that are 8mm in diameter and 300mm in length. They are also around 70 grams a piece, not the lighter weight which my understanding is for a shorter version. I was anticipating the extra weight since another reviewer gave meaningful and helpful feedback. I completely understand and agree with the criticisms expressed about the heavy weight and the high cost. I also don't think these are good for backpacking, possibly could work for staking down heavier things like EzUps or large canopies. These are SOLID and reflect that fact with heavy weight. I don't mind that they weigh a lot because I only plan to use two of these stakes for setting up a secure ridgeline across poles, with lighter weight stakes for the guylines.

The cordage loops at the end seem kind of cheap and low quality in comparison to the stakes themselves. The stake materials, welds and finishing all look great, although a couple stakes new-out-of-the-package have a slight curve/bend to them. There are no sharp edges or other apparent issues. Overall I'm very pleased.

The biggest issue is the large and rough seams in the middle from where the different colored strip on top meets the sides.
